specPoints.text: describe the generation of electricity by the rotation of a magnet within a coil of wire and of a coil of wire within a magnetic field, and describe the factors that affect the size of the induced voltage

primer.text: Spin a magnet in a coil — or a coil in a field — and rotation becomes electricity: the generator is induction put to work. This note covers both rotation arrangements, the three size factors, and the split-ring commutator that turns a dynamo's alternating induction into one-way direct delivery.

lessons.title: Generators: rotation into electricity
lessons.opening: A generator is induction industrialised: a coil spins in a magnetic field — or a magnet spins inside a coil — and the changing field induces a voltage. Because the rotation keeps changing the field's direction, the output voltage alternates, which is why generators are the AC sources of the grid.
keyPoints: Electricity is generated by rotating a magnet within a coil of wire.
Electricity is also generated by rotating a coil of wire inside a magnetic field.
The rotation changes the field through the coil, inducing a voltage.
The induced voltage alternates because the rotation reverses the field change each half turn.
Larger induced voltages come from faster rotation, stronger fields and more turns.

low.restatement: Spin a magnet inside a coil: the field through the coil swings one way then the other every turn, and the coil responds with an alternating voltage.
low.analogy: The spinning magnet is a wave-maker and the coil is the surfer: every sweep of the wave lifts the reading, one way then the other.
low.examPointer: Both arrangements score — magnet-in-coil AND coil-in-field — quote the one the diagram shows, not your favourite.

medium.restatement: Rotation makes the field threading the coil oscillate sinusoidally, so the induced voltage is alternating with the same period as the rotation. The 6.16 factor set — rotation speed, field strength, turn count — sets the amplitude, and the two mechanical arrangements (magnet in coil, coil in field) are electrically equivalent generators.
medium.analogy: A generator is a pump for charge: each half revolution pushes current round the circuit one way, then the next half pushes it back.
medium.examPointer: For 6-mark answers, chain rotation → changing field → induced voltage → alternating output, then close with the three amplitude factors.

check.stem: What does rotating a magnet inside a coil of wire generate?

options.text: an induced alternating voltage in the coil
options.explanation: Rotation changes the field and induction delivers voltage.
The rotating field reverses each half turn, so the output alternates.

options.text: a magnetic force on the coil
options.explanation: That is the motor effect; generation is induction.
The coil gains voltage, not permanent magnetism.

check.stem: Which arrangement also generates electricity by rotation?

options.text: rotating a coil of wire inside a magnetic field
options.explanation: Both 6.16 arrangements generate.

options.text: holding a coil still inside a steady field
options.explanation: No change means no induction.

options.text: sliding a magnet along beside the coil without entering
options.explanation: The field through the coil must change.

options.text: winding more wire but never moving anything
options.explanation: Turns scale the effect; motion is still required.

check.stem: Why is the generator's output voltage alternating?

options.text: the rotation reverses the field change every half turn
options.explanation: Each half turn flips the induced polarity.
Resistance is not the cause of alternation.

options.text: the magnet switches off twice per turn
options.explanation: The magnet stays magnetised; the field direction swings.
Heating is irrelevant to the alternation.

check.stem: Which change increases the size of a generator's induced voltage?

options.explanation: Faster change of field gives larger induced voltage.
Slower rotation gives a smaller voltage.

options.text: using fewer turns on the coil
options.explanation: Fewer turns reduce the summed voltage.
A weaker field gives a smaller voltage.

check.stem: A hand-cranked generator lights a lamp dimly at one crank speed. To brighten the lamp the student should:

options.text: crank faster to induce a larger voltage
options.explanation: More speed, more voltage, brighter lamp.
Slower cranking dims the lamp further.

options.text: remove turns from the generator coil
options.explanation: Fewer turns induce less voltage.
The lamp needs the circuit to glow at all.

check.stem: State the two rotation arrangements that generate electricity.
check.modelAnswer: Rotating a magnet inside a coil of wire, or rotating a coil of wire inside a magnetic field.

check.stem: State three factors that change how large a generator's induced voltage is.
check.modelAnswer: The speed of rotation, the strength of the magnetic field, and the number of turns on the coil.

check.stem: Explain why the induced voltage of a spinning-magnet generator changes direction twice per revolution.
check.modelAnswer: Each revolution carries the magnet's field through the coil one way, then the other: the field threading the coil grows, peaks, falls, and reverses as the magnet turns. The induced voltage follows the field change, so its polarity flips at the half-turn points — twice per revolution.

check.stem: A bicycle dynamo drives a lamp; the rider speeds up. Describe the change in the lamp's brightness and explain it by the generator factors.
check.modelAnswer: The lamp brightens. The faster wheel spins the generator's magnet faster, so the field through the coil changes more quickly and the induced voltage grows — a larger voltage drives a larger current through the lamp, making it brighter.

lessons.title: Dynamos: turning alternating output into direct
lessons.opening: A dynamo is a generator wired for direct current: the coil still induces an alternating voltage, but a split-ring commutator swaps the connections every half turn, so the output to the circuit always pushes the same way. Slip rings leave the alternation intact; the split ring flattens it.
keyPoints: A dynamo is a spinning coil in a magnetic field delivering direct current.
The coil itself still induces an alternating voltage.
A split-ring commutator swaps the external connection every half turn.
The swap cancels the alternation, so the circuit current flows one way only.
Slip rings, by contrast, pass the alternating output through unchanged.

low.restatement: Inside a dynamo the voltage alternates as the coil spins, but the split ring swaps the wires at each half turn, so the outside circuit always sees current flowing the same way.
low.analogy: A revolvng door attendant flips the exit signs twice a lap so every leaver leaves through the same door — the traffic outside flows one way.
low.examPointer: Keep the two contacts straight: slip rings give AC out, split ring gives DC out — swapping them is the classic error.

medium.restatement: The dynamo's induced coil voltage is inherently alternating; the commutator is a mechanical rectifier that reverses the external polarity synchronised with the coil's half turns. The delivered current is unidirectional but pulsating — the alternation is folded, not removed — while slip-ring contact preserves the true alternating output of an alternator.
medium.analogy: The split ring folds a zigzag road into a straight-looking one: the car still climbs and dips, but never turns back.
medium.examPointer: Say 'the coil's voltage is still alternating' before crediting the commutator — the raw induction is unchanged; only the delivery is rectified.

check.stem: What does a dynamo deliver to the external circuit?

options.text: direct current in one direction only
options.explanation: The split-ring commutator rectifies the output.
That is the alternator's slip-ring output.
The dynamo is a working generator.
The output is one-way by design.

check.stem: What does the split-ring commutator do in a dynamo?

options.text: swaps the external connection every half turn
options.explanation: The swap folds the alternation into one-way flow.
The coil keeps spinning; the contacts follow it.
The commutator reroutes; it never amplifies.

options.text: disconnects the circuit twice per turn
options.explanation: It swaps contacts; it does not break the circuit twice per turn as its purpose.

check.stem: The voltage induced IN the dynamo coil itself is:

options.text: alternating, as in any rotating generator
options.explanation: Rectification happens outside the coil, at the contacts.

options.text: direct current, because it is a dynamo
options.explanation: The DC label describes the delivery, not the coil voltage.
The spinning coil induces a real voltage.
The induced voltage oscillates with the rotation.

check.stem: Which component would you fit to keep the ALTERNATING output of a generator unchanged?

options.explanation: Slip rings pass the alternating output through untouched.
That rectifies the output into DC.
Extra field changes size, not the AC character.
Axle length is electrically irrelevant.

check.stem: The rotation of a dynamo speeds up. The lamp it feeds:

options.text: glows brighter, with current still flowing one way
options.explanation: Bigger induced voltage, same one-way delivery.
The commutator keeps the delivery one-way.
More rotation means more voltage, not none.
The induced voltage grows with speed.

check.stem: State the component that converts a generator's alternating output to direct.
check.modelAnswer: A split-ring commutator swaps the connection every half turn, delivering direct current.

check.stem: State what slip rings deliver that a split-ring commutator does not.
check.modelAnswer: Slip rings deliver the alternating current unchanged, while the commutator delivers one-way direct current.

check.stem: Explain why the dynamo's output current never reverses even though the coil's induced voltage does.
check.modelAnswer: Each half turn, the split-ring commutator swaps which brush connects to which coil end. When the coil's induced voltage reverses, the external connections have just been swapped too, so the reversal inside is cancelled outside: the circuit always sees the same polarity, and the current flows one way throughout.

check.stem: A bicycle lamp is fed first by a slip-ring alternator, then by a split-ring dynamo of the same coil and magnet. Compare the currents in the lamp circuit.
check.modelAnswer: With slip rings the lamp current alternates direction every half turn at the same frequency as the wheel. With the split-ring dynamo the current always flows the same way through the lamp, pulsing in size but never reversing. The peak sizes match — the same coil and magnet induce the same voltages — only the delivery differs.

glossary.definition: A device that induces a voltage by rotating a magnet in a coil or a coil in a field.
A generator whose split-ring commutator delivers one-way direct current.
Full-ring contacts that pass a generator's alternating output through unchanged.
